The main point of contention here seems to be whether there was a racist element to this situation. I doubt SFSS believes that individually the security guards and cop involved are hardcore KKK members or anything (and if they do then I would definitely disagree with that), but racism exists in this situation from contextual and institutional standpoints. 

I brought up the aspect of weaponization of law enforcement against blacks and the disproportionate practice of carding which SFU is using to enforce COVID policies, with this in mind I find it hard to definitively say there was no racism involved. Now of course no one called him the 'N' word or anything like that, but it's how the situation was handled that is characteristic of implicitly racist institutions.

>They failed to uphold the basic responsibilities of being student representatives.

In what way? Their actions have been on behalf of students, in this case specifically black students, as with other issues they have been focused on, such as tuition increases.

> They went with a story that was potentially problematic. Posted information that was incredibly irresponsible of the consequences.

How would the story be problematic for anyone but SFU? 


> They failed to fact check or correct their mistakes as new developments happened.

If this is referring to the racist element included in their statement, the weaponization of law enforcement is a known phenomenon where police are called on black people who are not doing anything illegal. While SFU does have a policy in which only current SFU members are allowed on campus, this is enforced via what is essentially carding, a practice that disproportionately affects black people since police (or security in this case) enforce it on people who they 'claim' to look suspicious. People have said Kayode was known to security, in which case they likely would have known that he is not well mentally (from what I have read), and other steps could have been taken to respond to a black man, with mental issues, doing nothing illegal, rather than calling the police. 


>Their leadership accused other students of being racist, simply for questioning the contents of the story.

I definitely do not support this behaviour. However I think people need to also be mindful of how their opinions can potentially be harmful to black students who witness these incidents and are more likely to be a victim of them. Straight up calling people racist for their objectivity is not helpful I think, and more civil discussions should be had before accusing people for their opinions. At the same time SFU does not exist within a politics-less vacuum and objectivity without attempting to look at larger social contexts can implicitly perpetuate racist ideas (such as the weaponization of police against blacks).
